newsitem.title: UK: British government, employers condemn work hours ruling.
newsitem.headline: British government, employers condemn work hours ruling.

text.p: Britain's government and leading employers joined forces on Tuesday to condemn the European Court of Justice's judgement that the UK must comply with rules limiting working hours.

The government's attack was led by Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind who told delegates attending the final day of the Confederation of British Industry's (CBI's) annual conference that he would work to change the ruling.
"We share your deep disappointment at this ruling...we'll obey the law and we'll work to change the law," he said.

CBI director general Adair Turner criticised the European Union's working time directive, which limits the working week to 48 hours, as "legislation at its worst: detailed, prescriptive regulations followed by extensive caveats and exemptions."
Smaller companies were seen as the biggest victims of Tuesday's judgement.
The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) said nearly half the UK's small companies employ people for more than 48 hours a week.

Andrew Buxton, chairman of Barclays Bank Plc, agreed. "Big companies will find it relatively easy to cope with this. It is certainly not over-concerning for Barclays. It's the small companies that will find this yet another piece of red tape."
But there were also fears the ruling would further worsen Britain's already tattered relations with the EU.

Prime Minister John Major signalled on Monday night that the government would not take the European Court's ruling lying down. He pledged to use Britain's veto to scupper progress at the InterGovernmental Conference (IGC) next year unless it got its way on working hours.
But an EU commissioner at the CBI conference said he hoped Britain would have a change of heart.
"I hope every member state, including the UK, would see the big disadvantages...of not taking a cooperative and active stance in negotiations," said Mario Monti, the EU internal market commissioner.

But Monti and business leaders pointed to loopholes in the directive as a way out for Britain, which views its flexible working practices as a major lure for foreign investors and a key factor in creating jobs.
The CBI immediately suggested a raft of ways for the government to get round the court ruling, including allowing the 48-hour week to be averaged over periods of six or even 12 months.

The annual employers' lobby meeting, which also heard Bank of England Governor Eddie George warn on Tuesday that British interest rates may have to rise further, was otherwise dominated by Europe both inside and outside the conference hall.

But most speakers from the main political parties stressed the need for Britain to stay firmly within Europe, while hanging on to its perceived competitive advantages, in particular labour market flexibility and the Social Chapter opt out.
Only a few speakers adopted an anti-European line, notably John Redwood, a Eurosceptic and Conservative politician.
He said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl "wants to build a country called Europe, governed from a city called Brussels with its economy directed from a bank in Frankfurt."

But a CBI survey on Sunday showed that a majority of Britain's business leaders now support the principle of a single currency, and there was clear exasperation with the increasingly Euro-sceptical line followed by the government.

BCC president David Richardson told the conference that politicians "should stop playing games with our future in Europe," adding the business view is that "we are in, we are right to be in, and that we should stay in."
He said Britain needed a government which is committed to Europe (and) is influential in the key decisions that affect Europe."
